title: Collibra slide visual grammar suite
purpose: Give presentation and document producers a shared way to choose visual form from reader intent, while leaving medium-specific geometry and delivery to the consuming library.
principles: Choose the visual grammar from the reader question before choosing a shell or atom.
Give every slide one dominant job and one obvious reading direction.
Use shape, position, line treatment, and text as meaning; color is supporting evidence.
Prefer a named grammar with a distinct rhythm over a renamed card or rectangle grid.
Carry source, scope, uncertainty, ownership, and next action where the claim needs them.
Translate the grammar across media without pretending that geometry or delivery is universal.
Split dense stories into a sequence of complementary slides instead of shrinking the type.

shell_roles.purpose: Orient the reader with a strong title, promise, and focal mark.
shell_roles.composition: Use a spacious field with one anchored statement and restrained supporting context.

shell_roles.purpose: Hold a narrative claim beside evidence, context, or a source note.
shell_roles.composition: Use an asymmetric rail and a visual field so the eye has a deliberate entry point.
avoid: a rail that repeats the headline

shell_roles.purpose: Give a bounded measure or signal room to be interpreted.
shell_roles.composition: Pair one measure with context, comparison, source, and implication.

shell_roles.purpose: Invite one bounded audience response with an explicit participation method.
shell_roles.composition: Use an open prompt field with one focal cue, a concise question, response lenses, and a printed handoff instruction.
avoid: a question without a response method
generic option cards with no facilitation cue

shell_roles.purpose: Make a meaningful difference between alternatives or states inspectable.
shell_roles.composition: Use a declared comparison axis and a visible bridge, delta, or decision cue.
avoid: two unrelated cards called before and after

shell_roles.purpose: Show movement through phases, owners, or handoffs.
shell_roles.composition: Give sequence a direction and make gates, owners, and exceptions visible.
avoid: a timeline that has no time or sequence meaning

shell_roles.purpose: Help a reader choose, prioritize, or resolve a trade-off.
shell_roles.composition: Expose the decision axes, threshold, or focal question before listing options.
avoid: a decorative diamond with no branch meaning

shell_roles.purpose: Explain a system, relationship, boundary, or operating model.
shell_roles.composition: Use semantic shapes, directional connectors, and a concise legend or key.

shell_roles.purpose: Let a reader inspect structured evidence without losing the conclusion.
shell_roles.composition: Use row, column, or lane structure only when it matches the comparison contract.
avoid: a table used as a default layout
dense cells without a reading order

grammars.name: Thesis field
grammars.reader_question: What is the one conclusion the reader should carry forward?
grammars.visual_language: A dominant statement sits in an open field with one evidence anchor and a clear implication.
grammars.reading_order: thesis to evidence to implication

medium_translation.slides: Use a native cover or hero shell with one strong statement and a restrained evidence mark.
medium_translation.docs: Open a section with the conclusion, then place supporting evidence in the next reading block.
medium_translation.sheets: Use a summary tab or top panel that points to the underlying evidence range.
medium_translation.web: Use a hero region with an accessible heading, supporting proof, and a direct next action.
medium_translation.exported_media: Keep the statement and source legible without narration or hover behavior.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The conclusion is available as heading text and the evidence relationship is repeated in prose.
grammars.evidence_contract: Name the source and scope of the evidence anchor; do not imply causation from a single signal.
avoid: a background image that carries the claim

grammars.name: Metric beacon
grammars.reader_question: What does this measure mean, and what should change because of it?
grammars.visual_language: One prominent measure is surrounded by context, comparison, and an implication cue.
grammars.reading_order: measure to context to implication

medium_translation.slides: Use a metric stage with a visible unit, comparison point, period, and source note.
medium_translation.docs: Lead with the measure in a callout, then explain denominator, period, and implication in text.
medium_translation.sheets: Keep the metric tied to its source range and expose the comparison formula or target.
medium_translation.web: Use a labeled metric component with a text alternative and an inspectable source link.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print the unit, period, and status cue next to the number rather than relying on color.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The number, unit, period, comparison, and status are all written in text.
grammars.evidence_contract: Declare denominator, time context, source, and whether the measure is actual, target, or estimate.
avoid: precision that the source does not support

grammars.name: Comparison split
grammars.reader_question: What materially differs between the current state and the alternative?
grammars.visual_language: Two states share a declared axis and are connected by a visible delta or bridge.
grammars.reading_order: comparison axis to current to alternative to delta

medium_translation.slides: Use a split frame, state columns, or a bridge that names the migration or decision between them.
medium_translation.docs: Use paired headings and a written transition paragraph instead of two isolated panels.
medium_translation.sheets: Place comparable fields in aligned columns and calculate the delta in a labeled column.
medium_translation.web: Use a comparison component with headings, semantic differences, and an accessible alternative.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print both state labels and the change cue so the relationship survives grayscale or cropping.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The axis and delta are stated in text, with state labels that do not depend on fill color.
grammars.evidence_contract: Identify the comparison basis, date or version, and whether the target is proposed or evidenced.
avoid: before and after labels without a transition

grammars.name: Journey spine
grammars.reader_question: How does an experience change from entry through outcome?
grammars.visual_language: A directional experience rail connects stages, friction, opportunity, and an outcome.
grammars.reading_order: entry to stages to friction to opportunity to outcome

medium_translation.slides: Use a rail with stage markers, experience notes, and a terminal outcome rather than a generic process row.
medium_translation.docs: Use stage headings with a consistent entry, experience, and opportunity pattern.
medium_translation.sheets: Keep stages as rows and experience dimensions as columns with explicit status text.
medium_translation.web: Use a semantic list or stepper with text-first stage content and optional visual emphasis.
medium_translation.exported_media: Keep stage names and friction or opportunity cues readable when the rail is viewed as a static image.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The journey is a labeled ordered list in the same order as the visual rail.
grammars.evidence_contract: Separate observed experience from proposed opportunity and name the research or source context.
avoid: a roadmap relabeled as a journey
stage names without lived quality or friction

grammars.name: Phase chevrons
grammars.reader_question: What sequence of phases moves the work toward the outcome?
grammars.visual_language: Directional phase forms create a forward path with gates, owners, and a terminal outcome.
grammars.reading_order: first phase to later phase to gate to outcome

medium_translation.slides: Use chevrons or stations for future sequence, with labels that distinguish phases from milestones.
medium_translation.docs: Use numbered sections or headings with explicit entry and exit conditions.
medium_translation.sheets: Use columns for phases and rows for owners, deliverables, gates, or dates.
medium_translation.web: Use an ordered step pattern with progress semantics only when progress is measured.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print sequence labels, phase names, and gate conditions directly on or beside the path.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The sequence is expressed as an ordered list with phase names and gate text.
grammars.evidence_contract: Mark future intent separately from completed evidence and identify the owner of each gate.

grammars.name: Governance orbit
grammars.reader_question: Which forums and owners keep the decision or operating model aligned?
grammars.visual_language: Forums, owners, and outcomes orbit a central decision or operating purpose.
grammars.reading_order: central purpose to forum to owner to outcome

medium_translation.slides: Use an orbit or spoke composition when alignment around a shared decision matters more than chronology.
medium_translation.docs: Use a central purpose statement followed by forum and owner subsections.
medium_translation.sheets: Use a cadence table with forums as rows, periods as columns, and decisions in the cells.
medium_translation.web: Use a hub-and-spoke or grouped list with visible ownership and cadence labels.
medium_translation.exported_media: Keep every spoke named and provide a linear reading order beside the radial view.

grammars.accessibility_cue: Every forum and owner is listed in a linear alternative with its outcome and cadence.
grammars.evidence_contract: Distinguish an existing governance commitment from a proposed operating model.
avoid: orbits with no central decision or ownership

grammars.name: Evidence chain
grammars.reader_question: How does the source evidence support the claim and the next action?
grammars.visual_language: Sources, observations, synthesis, and action are linked in a directional chain.
grammars.reading_order: source to observation to claim to action

medium_translation.slides: Use labeled links or evidence cards that keep source context beside the claim rather than in a footnote only.
medium_translation.docs: Use a claim heading, evidence block, limitation note, and action paragraph.
medium_translation.sheets: Keep source fields and transformations adjacent to the result or in an inspectable provenance tab.
medium_translation.web: Use expandable evidence details or linked source notes while preserving a visible summary.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print source kind, confidence or limitation, and action cue in the static composition.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The chain is repeated as a sequence of labeled text blocks with source and uncertainty included.
grammars.evidence_contract: Never collapse source, interpretation, and recommendation into one undifferentiated card.
avoid: source notes detached from the claims they support

grammars.name: Quadrant field
grammars.reader_question: How do options compare across the two decision dimensions that matter?
grammars.visual_language: A plotted field makes axes, thresholds, clusters, and outliers visible.
grammars.reading_order: axis labels to regions to plotted option to recommendation

medium_translation.slides: Use a plotted field with named axes, a legend, and a callout for the decision implication.
medium_translation.docs: Use an axis explanation followed by a compact option table and recommendation.
medium_translation.sheets: Keep axis definitions, values, and plotted labels in adjacent source ranges.
medium_translation.web: Use an accessible scatter or matrix alternative with filterable option details.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print axis names, scale meaning, option labels, and recommendation outside the plot marks.

grammars.accessibility_cue: Every option has a text row with its two values, region, and decision implication.
grammars.evidence_contract: Name the measurement basis and explain whether placement is observed, estimated, or judgmental.
avoid: placing options by decoration rather than a stated rule

grammars.name: Pyramid stack
grammars.reader_question: Which foundations support the higher-order outcome?
grammars.visual_language: Stacked layers narrow or broaden to show dependency, maturity, or abstraction.
grammars.reading_order: foundation to enabling layer to outcome

medium_translation.slides: Use trapezoid or banded layers with one claim per layer and an explicit outcome at the apex.
medium_translation.docs: Use ordered headings that explain why each foundation enables the next layer.
medium_translation.sheets: Use a dependency table with layer, prerequisite, owner, and evidence columns.
medium_translation.web: Use a nested or stacked list with semantic headings and clear dependency language.
medium_translation.exported_media: Keep layer labels, direction, and foundation-to-outcome reading order visible without color.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The layers are provided as an ordered list from foundation to outcome.
grammars.evidence_contract: State whether each layer is an existing capability, a dependency, or a proposed investment.
avoid: a stack with equal claims in every band
using a pyramid only as decoration

grammars.name: Hierarchy tree
grammars.reader_question: How does one focal concept decompose into named child concepts across explicit levels?
grammars.visual_language: A bounded rooted tree uses level bands and parent-child branches to make decomposition legible from root to leaf.
grammars.reading_order: root to level band to branch to leaf to relationship key

medium_translation.slides: Use a top-down tree with visible level bands, parent-child connectors, printed root/branch/leaf cues, and a concise relationship key.
medium_translation.docs: Use nested headings or an indented outline that preserves the root-to-leaf order and names the relationship.
medium_translation.sheets: Use one row per node with level, parent, order, detail, and evidence fields so the tree can be reconstructed and audited.
medium_translation.web: Use a semantic nested list or expandable tree with an equivalent linear reading order and visible relationship labels.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print level labels, relationship meaning, source context, and unknown status so branching is not the only cue.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The tree is repeated as a level-ordered text list in root-to-leaf order, including parent relationships and unknown status.
grammars.evidence_contract: Name the source and scope of the decomposition; distinguish observed structure from proposed or unresolved child concepts.
avoid: unlabeled connectors or unbounded node density

grammars.name: Waterfall bridge
grammars.reader_question: Which positive and negative contributions explain the movement from start to finish?
grammars.visual_language: A starting measure is bridged through labeled contributions to a final measure.
grammars.reading_order: start to contribution to contribution to finish

medium_translation.slides: Use a waterfall or bridge with printed values, direction, and a concise takeaway.
medium_translation.docs: Use an ordered change list with a start, signed contributors, and finish statement.
medium_translation.sheets: Expose the source values and running total so the bridge can be audited.
medium_translation.web: Use a chart with a table alternative and a clear distinction between contributors and totals.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print signs, units, and start or finish labels; do not rely on up or down color alone.

grammars.accessibility_cue: Each contribution has a signed text value and the running sequence is available as a table.
grammars.evidence_contract: The start, contributors, and finish must reconcile to the declared total within the source precision.
avoid: floating bars with no baseline meaning

grammars.name: Swimlane handoff
grammars.reader_question: Who acts when, where does work cross a boundary, and what decision gates it?
grammars.visual_language: Owner lanes carry a directional sequence with explicit handoffs, decisions, and exceptions.
grammars.reading_order: lane to sequence to handoff to decision

medium_translation.slides: Use lanes and orthogonal connectors with printed handoff labels and decision gates.
medium_translation.docs: Use owner subsections or a responsibility table followed by the exception path.
medium_translation.sheets: Use owners as rows or columns and steps as ordered fields with a handoff marker.
medium_translation.web: Use a semantic process list grouped by owner with explicit state and exception text.
medium_translation.exported_media: Keep lane names, action verbs, connector meaning, and decision text legible in a static view.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The visual is paired with a lane-first ordered list of actions and handoffs.
grammars.evidence_contract: Mark assumed ownership, observed flow, and proposed control points separately.
avoid: a process row that hides ownership

grammars.name: Network hub
grammars.reader_question: Which relationships or dependencies surround the shared outcome?
grammars.visual_language: A named focal outcome connects to a bounded set of related actors, systems, or dependencies.
grammars.reading_order: outcome to connected node to relationship label

medium_translation.slides: Use a hub-and-spoke field with relationship labels and a bounded node count.
medium_translation.docs: Use a focal outcome paragraph followed by relationship subsections or a table.
medium_translation.sheets: Use a source edge list with node names, relationship labels, and evidence columns.
medium_translation.web: Use a graph only when a keyboard and text alternative expose the same relationships.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print relationship labels and provide a linear key so proximity is not the only meaning.

grammars.accessibility_cue: Every relationship is written as an outcome-to-node statement with its label.
grammars.evidence_contract: Do not imply a live organizational or system graph when the inputs are illustrative or stale.
avoid: network density that hides the focal outcome

grammars.name: Radial wheel
grammars.reader_question: Which dimensions or capabilities must work together around the focal purpose?
grammars.visual_language: A central purpose is surrounded by complementary dimensions that form a bounded system.
grammars.reading_order: center to dimension to supporting detail

medium_translation.slides: Use a wheel or ring when the dimensions are co-dependent rather than sequential.
medium_translation.docs: Use a central purpose followed by dimension headings in a consistent order.
medium_translation.sheets: Use one row per dimension with status, owner, evidence, and dependency fields.
medium_translation.web: Use a grouped list or accessible radial enhancement with a clear text-first order.
medium_translation.exported_media: Include the center label, dimension names, and a linear reading key beside the wheel.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The dimensions are enumerated in a stable order with their supporting detail.
grammars.evidence_contract: Use a status or maturity cue for each dimension and label unknown or incomplete coverage.

grammars.name: State ladder
grammars.reader_question: How does one artifact, capability, or operating state move through maturity or refinement?
grammars.visual_language: Named states form a directional ladder with promotion conditions and a terminal quality bar.
grammars.reading_order: current state to gate to next state to target state

medium_translation.slides: Use a ladder or refinement ribbon with explicit gate text and a property or evidence alternative.
medium_translation.docs: Use state headings with entry condition, exit condition, and owner fields.
medium_translation.sheets: Use a state transition table with conditions, evidence, and accountable owner.
medium_translation.web: Use a stepper or state list that exposes the same conditions without animation.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print state names and transition conditions; do not imply promotion from color or height alone.

grammars.accessibility_cue: Each state and gate is written as a sequence with explicit transition conditions.
grammars.evidence_contract: Separate current evidence, proposed target, and unverified promotion criteria.
avoid: a progress bar that implies measured progress

grammars.name: Narrative rail
grammars.reader_question: How should a message, evidence, and action be read together?
grammars.visual_language: A strong message rail guides the eye through selected evidence and a next-action cue.
grammars.reading_order: message to selected evidence to next action

medium_translation.slides: Use an editorial rail or storyboard with varied emphasis instead of equal-weight cards.
medium_translation.docs: Use a pull quote or key message followed by evidence and an action paragraph.
medium_translation.sheets: Use a summary row linked to a detail range and mark the selected evidence fields.
medium_translation.web: Use a content rail with headings, citations, and a visible next action.
medium_translation.exported_media: Keep the message, source, and action together so the story survives as a single page.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The message and evidence are available as sequential headings and paragraphs.
grammars.evidence_contract: Quotes and emphasis retain attribution, context, and any uncertainty that changes interpretation.

grammars.name: Participation prompt
grammars.reader_question: What should the audience respond to, and how should they participate?
grammars.visual_language: A focal participation cue opens into one answerable prompt, a small set of response lenses, and an explicit action handoff.
grammars.reading_order: participation mode to prompt to response lenses to action handoff

medium_translation.slides: Use a spacious prompt field with a visible mode cue, numbered response lenses, and the exact action the room should take.
medium_translation.docs: Use a question heading followed by response guidance, a bounded set of lenses, and a written submission or discussion instruction.
medium_translation.sheets: Place the prompt above a labeled response range and keep the allowed response method, owner, and review state visible.
medium_translation.web: Use a semantic question region with labeled controls, clear submission behavior, keyboard access, and a non-interactive fallback.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print the participation mode, prompt, response lenses, and action instruction so the cue remains usable without interaction.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The participation mode, prompt, response lenses, and action are available in one linear text order and do not depend on color or motion.
grammars.evidence_contract: Distinguish a facilitation prompt from collected evidence; do not imply that audience responses were received unless the source and collection state are supplied.
avoid: an open question with no response instruction
participation encoded only by animation or color
source-deck people, imagery, or response data carried into a reusable example

grammars.name: Data table lens
grammars.reader_question: What should the reader notice in this structured evidence, and why?
grammars.visual_language: A constrained table or matrix is paired with a narrative lens that highlights the decision-relevant pattern.
grammars.reading_order: lens to table headers to notable rows or cells to implication

medium_translation.slides: Use a compact table with a narrative rail, meaningful row labels, and a highlighted pattern.
medium_translation.docs: Use a short table only after explaining the question and how to read it.
medium_translation.sheets: Use filters, frozen headers, source fields, and a summary view that names the lens.
medium_translation.web: Use a responsive table with an accessible summary and a row or cell focus treatment.
medium_translation.exported_media: Keep headers, units, source, and the selected pattern readable; split dense detail into an appendix.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The lens is stated in text and the table has row-first or column-first reading guidance.
grammars.evidence_contract: Show units, time context, source, and missingness; do not let an accent cell carry a conclusion alone.

grammars.name: Collage mosaic
grammars.reader_question: What collection of visual evidence makes the story tangible?
grammars.visual_language: A small set of images, marks, or artifacts is composed as an intentional editorial mosaic with captions.
grammars.reading_order: thesis to artifact to caption to pattern

medium_translation.slides: Use a bounded collage with deliberate focal hierarchy, captions, and reviewed asset provenance.
medium_translation.docs: Use figures with captions and an explanatory paragraph rather than decorative image clusters.
medium_translation.sheets: Keep asset references and captions in a catalog range; use images only as reviewed evidence.
medium_translation.web: Use a responsive gallery with alt text, captions, loading behavior, and rights metadata.
medium_translation.exported_media: Embed captions and source context so the static image set is interpretable on its own.

grammars.accessibility_cue: Every artifact has alt text or a written description and a caption in reading order.
grammars.evidence_contract: Record source, usage authority, version, and review status for every shared or external asset.
avoid: image walls that substitute mood for evidence

grammars.name: Chart plot
grammars.reader_question: What comparison, trend, distribution, or relationship does the data support?
grammars.visual_language: A data-native plot is paired with annotation, units, source context, and a text or table alternative.
grammars.reading_order: question to measure to pattern to source

medium_translation.slides: Use the chart family that matches the question and keep the takeaway, units, and source near the plot.
medium_translation.docs: Use a figure with a plain-language takeaway and a tabular or textual alternative.
medium_translation.sheets: Keep the chart bound to labeled data ranges and expose a source or calculation tab.
medium_translation.web: Use accessible axes, summaries, focusable data, and a downloadable or textual alternative.
medium_translation.exported_media: Print labels, units, legend meaning, time context, and source; avoid hover-only detail.

grammars.accessibility_cue: The chart has a text summary and data alternative; color is not the only series distinction.
grammars.evidence_contract: Name scale, units, time context, source, and uncertainty or missingness where relevant.
avoid: decorative chart shapes that distort the data

rhythm_rules.rule: Give the page one dominant reader job and let supporting evidence serve that job.
rhythm_rules.why: A library becomes reusable when a maker can choose a form from intent instead of arranging content by habit.
rhythm_rules.failure_signal: The title, visual, and action each ask the reader to do something different.

rhythm_rules.rule: Create a deliberate visual entry point before adding secondary detail.
rhythm_rules.why: Asymmetric emphasis and focal signals make varied compositions easier to scan.
rhythm_rules.failure_signal: Every object has equal visual weight or the eye has no stable first stop.

rhythm_rules.rule: Across a story, alternate visual grammars when the reader question changes.
rhythm_rules.why: A one-deck library should demonstrate how a narrative moves, not repeat one layout for every beat.
rhythm_rules.failure_signal: Adjacent pages share the same shell, primitive, and reading rhythm without a semantic reason.

rhythm_rules.rule: Split dense evidence into a complementary detail page before reducing type or label clarity.
rhythm_rules.why: Readable evidence is more valuable than fitting every input into one canvas.
rhythm_rules.failure_signal: The visual depends on tiny labels, unexplained abbreviations, or crowded connectors.

rhythm_rules.rule: Open and close a multi-page story with orientation and a named implication or action.
rhythm_rules.why: A library deck is an editorial object, not only a catalog of isolated examples.
rhythm_rules.failure_signal: The reader reaches the final page without knowing what to remember or do next.

rhythm_rules.rule: Before inviting audience input, reduce information density and make the response method and handoff explicit.
rhythm_rules.why: Participation works when the room can see the question, how to respond, and what will happen to the response.
rhythm_rules.failure_signal: The prompt competes with dense evidence, assumes an unstated interaction, or leaves the audience unsure what to do.

accessibility: Preserve a linear reading order for every visual grammar.
Keep color, position, shape, and motion from carrying meaning alone.
Provide text alternatives for charts, diagrams, imagery, and plotted relationships.
Keep labels, units, source context, and uncertainty inspectable at the intended medium.
Test content expansion, contrast, smallest supported view, and static export behavior.
Use reduced-motion behavior when a consumer adds transitions to an otherwise static grammar.

provenance.notes: Extends the visual capability catalog with a slide-specific reader-question and cross-medium contract.
Reuses semantic roles for diagram, workflow, chart, state, evidence, and uncertainty meaning.
The native slide contract owns template inheritance and geometry; this suite owns visual intent and translation rules.
Pattern diversity, composition recipes, and reader-first sequencing inform the concepts without importing code, assets, or text.
